Geotechnical Staff Engineer

GeotechStaffEngineer

User Manual for the practicing geotechnical engineer
A toolkit that turns the staff engineer’s repertoire into composable, machine-callable methods, wraps them in a probabilistic variability engine, and drives them with an engine-agnostic reasoning agent — because in geotechnical engineering the true answer is a distribution, not a single number.
Version 5.35.0
36 analysis modules · 35 digitized references · 1598 agent-callable methods
FOSM / PEM / Monte Carlo / FORM reliability · validated against published benchmarks

Professional-use disclaimer

Read this first

GeotechStaffEngineer is an analysis and research aid — a multiplier for a qualified engineer’s judgment, not a replacement for it, and not a design deliverable.

Geotechnical engineering is the practice of building on and in the ground, where the material is the earth itself: heterogeneous, layered, partly saturated, and sampled at only a handful of points across a site. Because the ground is variable and only partly known, a single number is never the answer. This toolkit exists to help an engineer run the industry-standard methods repeatedly across plausible subsurface and loading conditions and understand the range and spread of answers. It does not know your site, and it cannot exercise engineering judgment.

What this software is — and is not

  • It is a library of deterministic methods, a probabilistic variability engine, digitized references, and an LLM agent that drives them.
  • It is not a stamped design, a professional opinion, or a substitute for site-specific investigation, characterization, and review.
  • Using this software creates no engineer-of-record relationship and no professional engagement with the authors or contributors.

Your responsibilities as a user

  • A qualified, licensed professional engineer familiar with the site must independently review every input, assumption, method selection, and result before it is relied upon. Outputs are candidate calculations to be checked, not conclusions to be adopted.
  • Confirm that the method applies to your problem. Every method has applicability limits, sign conventions, and edge cases — documented in each module’s DESIGN.md (and, where present, VALIDATION.md).
  • Confirm the inputs and units. All quantities are SI (meters, kPa, kN, kN/m, degrees). Mixed or mis-scaled units are the user’s responsibility to catch.
  • Treat LLM-agent output with particular care. The agent can select the wrong method, mis-transcribe a value, or read a chart imperfectly. Its answers are a starting point for review, never a final basis for design.

Validation scope

Selected modules are validated against published worked examples and benchmarks (Fredlund & Krahn 1977, ACADS, Duncan, Griffiths & Lane, the Prandtl solution, and GEC / Caltrans / FLAC examples). The specific problems checked and their verdicts are recorded in validation_examples/RESULTS.md and the per-module VALIDATION.md files. Validation covers only those documented cases. Agreement on a benchmark does not certify correctness for any other geometry, parameter range, or loading condition.

No warranty

This software is provided under the MIT License “AS IS”, WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND, express or implied. In no event shall the authors or copyright holders be liable for any claim, damages, or other liability arising from its use. Responsibility for the safety, adequacy, and code-compliance of any design remains entirely with the licensed professional engineer who adopts it.

Chapter 1What this package is

Geotechnical engineering is the practice of building on and in the ground — foundations, retaining walls, slopes, excavations, embankments. Unlike a steel beam with a certified strength, the geotechnical engineer’s material is the earth itself: heterogeneous, layered, partly saturated, and sampled at only a handful of points across an entire site. Because the ground is variable and only partly known, a single number is never the answer.

Understanding a geotechnical problem means understanding how the answer moves as the inputs move. Analysis is repeated calculation across plausible subsurface and loading conditions — running a chained assortment of industry-standard formulas, empirical correlations, and numerical methods, comparing against the design requirements, and varying assumptions until the design is robust across the uncertainty. The engineer’s job is to understand the range and spread of answers, not one point estimate. The true answer is a distribution.

1.1 What a geotechnical engineer actually does

StepActivityReality
CharacterizeDrill borings, push CPT cones, run lab testsA sparse, noisy picture of strength, stiffness, and groundwater — never the whole truth
IdealizeCollapse the data into a layered soil profileDesign values of φ, c, γ, water table — each an estimate with a spread
AnalyzeRun the method (bearing, settlement, pile, slope)A chained assortment of standard formulas and numerical methods
Check & reviseCompare to requirements; vary assumptions; re-runLoop until the design is robust across the uncertainty

Steps 3 and 4 are repeated calculations across plausible conditions. This toolkit packages those methods as clean, machine-callable Python and puts a reasoning agent on top so the engineer can explore more of the problem in the time they have.

1.2 The lineage: every tool amplified the engineer

Slide rules and design charts → spreadsheets and FEM → scripting and Monte Carlo → LLM agents. Every tool in this lineage did the same thing: it let one engineer explore more of the problem. This project is the next step — not a replacement for judgment, but a multiplier for it. Take the methods a staff engineer uses, make every one a clean function that returns structured data, wrap the variability tooling around them, and drive them with an agent that reads the standards back to you.

1.3 The architecture in four layers

One stack, layered so each concern stays independent:

LayerWhat it isWhy it’s separate
Agent harnessAn engine-agnostic LLM driver (funhouse_agent) that discovers modules, calls methods, reads figures, and cites references; the chat web app (webapp, two pages: GeotechStaffEngineer and Document Review); and below both the shared core aec-agent-core (model connections, vision calls, guards and records, Word and Excel), a separate package this one pins exactlyThe reasoning that combines methods lives here, not inside the methods
Variability enginereliability — FOSM, PEM, Monte Carlo, FORM → β and Pf, plus a published COV database and spatial averagingOrthogonal: it wraps any deterministic method as a callable and characterizes how its output scatters
Deterministic analysisThe analysis modules — dataclass in, dataclass out, one method per engineering problemIndependent, testable leaves; no analysis module imports another
Shared spine + referencesgeotech_common’s SoilProfile that every module speaks, and the digitized reference libraryOne way to describe the ground; one place to cite the standards
The design rule that makes outputs citable

Everything is SI (m, kPa, kN, kN/m, degrees). Every analyze_*() returns a dataclass with .summary() for human/agent reading and .to_dict() for JSON. Analysis modules never import each other — the routing that combines them lives in the agent layer. That discipline is what lets a result be traced, reviewed, and cited.

Chapter 2Installation & environments

2.1 Install from PyPI

# the whole stack: analysis modules, reference library, deep agent, webapp
pip install geotech-staff-engineer

# Document Review alone, with nothing geotechnical (a separate package)
pip install aec-document-review

The plain install already covers the native modules — bearing capacity, settlement, piles, walls, slope stability, the reliability engine, fem2d, and the reference library (geotech-references is a hard dependency, so DM7/GEC/UFC lookups work out of the box). It also brings two other packages of the same project: the shared core aec-agent-core (pinned exactly) and planlens. Since 5.8.1 the plain install also brings the third-party libraries the wrapper modules drive; the extra names below ([deep], [full] and the rest) are kept as empty aliases so old install lines still work. Three extras still add a package: [ags4] and [subsurface] (python-ags4) and [pydiggs].

Honest failure when an extra is missing

A method whose backend is not installed (python-ags4 or pydiggs without their extra) fails cleanly with a “not installed” message rather than a confusing traceback; a library a host cannot install (PyNiteFEA on numpy 1.26) leaves its tool out.

2.3 Local Python

Requires Python 3.11 or newer (the shared core and deepagents need it). The package is pure Python; the only heavy dependencies are numpy and scipy. For the LLM agent you need an engine (see the next chapter) and, for a Claude engine, an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment. Keys are read from the environment at run time — never pass them through a notebook cell or a chat transcript.

2.4 The chat web app

The install includes the Streamlit chat app: two pages over one shell, Document Review (the app root) and GeotechStaffEngineer (/geotech). Its files are inside the installed package, so point Streamlit at them:

streamlit run "$(python -c 'import webapp, os; print(os.path.dirname(webapp.__file__))')/pages_entry.py"

Put app.py in place of pages_entry.py for the geotech page alone; in Windows PowerShell write \pages_entry.py after the closing parenthesis. Databricks, Foundry and the app’s settings are in the repository’s webapp/README.md.

2.5 Databricks / Funhouse

Install from a cluster-accessible location — /tmp or a Unity Catalog Volume, not /Workspace (the workspace FUSE mount mangles wheel filenames and does not durably store output files):

%pip install "geotech-staff-engineer"
# or a test wheel uploaded to /tmp or a UC Volume; when the test set carries
# the core's wheel too, put it on the same line:
%pip install "/tmp/geotech_staff_engineer-<ver>-py3-none-any.whl" "/tmp/aec_agent_core-<core ver>-py3-none-any.whl"
No compiled meshing dependency

The cross-section and RC-section engines used to wrap sectionproperties and concreteproperties, which both require cytriangle — a compiled wheel corporate package proxies quarantine. A Nexus malware-defense 403 on it failed the entire 5.12.0 install on the cluster, so in 5.13.0 both were re-implemented natively on numpy/scipy: exact closed-form integration for the geometry, published closed forms for torsion, and ACI strain compatibility for the RC section. The retired libraries’ outputs were pinned as regression oracles first; every RC scalar agrees to better than 0.04%.

The typing_extensions / restart-Python note (now handled automatically)

Databricks cluster runtimes pre-import an old typing_extensions (<4.13) at kernel startup, which used to break the langgraph imports behind the [deep] agent with TypeError: TypedDict() got an unexpected keyword argument 'extra_items', requiring dbutils.library.restartPython(). As of v5.4 the package repairs this in place: ensure_typing_extensions() (in the shared core’s aec_agent_core.runtime_check; the old name funhouse_agent.runtime_check is an alias) runs automatically at the top of the first funhouse_agent.deep import, reloading the freshly-installed typing_extensions≥4.13 so the restart is normally no longer needed. If an even older copy is pinned at cluster scope and the in-place reload can’t win, it raises a clear message that falls back to the restart instruction.

Save calc packages, DXF, and plots to /tmp or a UC Volume and copy them out with dbutils.fs.cp; writes to /Workspace can silently leave an 11-byte placeholder. As of recent releases the file tools defend themselves — they verify the written bytes and return a rescue_path in /tmp if the target did not store the content.

2.6 Reference figures: GEOTECH_REFERENCES_DOCS

The reference figure catalogs (captions, page numbers, cross-links) ship inside the wheel, so figure_search works from a clean install. The source PDF pages are not shipped (large + license). To enable the vision read-off — where the agent renders a catalogued chart and reads a value off it — place the reference PDFs in a folder and set GEOTECH_REFERENCES_DOCS to point at it. On Databricks, copy a docs/ folder of PDFs in and set the variable.

Chapter 3Using the agent

The same validated methods are reachable at three altitudes: import a module and get a dataclass back; wrap that method to return the distribution; or describe the problem in natural language and let the agent run the methods and cite the standards. This chapter is about the third altitude — the agent.

3.1 The v1 agent: GeotechAgent

GeotechAgent is engine-agnostic: it drives any backend that satisfies the small GenAIEngine protocol (a chat() method, optionally analyze_image() for vision). Ship it a Claude engine, a Funhouse PrompterAPI, or a native OpenAI-tool-calling engine.

from funhouse_agent import GeotechAgent, ClaudeEngine, NativeToolEngine

# Claude (reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment)
agent = GeotechAgent(genai_engine=ClaudeEngine())

# Databricks / Funhouse with native OpenAI tool calling (recommended there)
agent = GeotechAgent(genai_engine=NativeToolEngine(fh_prompter))

result = agent.ask("2 m strip footing, 1.5 m deep, sand phi=30, c=10, water at 5 m. "
                   "Bearing capacity and FOS - and how sensitive is it to phi? Cite the method.")
print(result.answer)        # the cited answer
print(result.tool_calls)    # every method the agent ran
print(result.rounds)        # ReAct iterations

3.2 How tool dispatch works

The agent never has to know a method signature in advance. It discovers the toolbox with four dispatch tools, then calls the one it needs:

ToolWhat it returns
list_agents()Every available module with a one-line brief
list_methods(agent, category)The methods on a module, grouped by category
describe_method(agent, method)Full parameter documentation — names, types, required flags, allowed values
call_agent(agent, method, params)Execute the calculation; returns the result dict or a helpful error

The dispatch layer is forgiving by design: a method name the model guesses is resolved through a curated alias map; a value that belongs to a selector parameter (say 'vesic') is redirected to the right call with a directive error; and a genuinely unknown name gets a “did you mean” suggestion. This cut the method-name guessing that otherwise dogs tool-using agents.

3.3 References through a scoped consultant

The primary agent does not call the reference modules directly. Reference access is routed through a single consult_references tool backed by a reference-scoped sub-agent — a second GeotechAgent restricted to the reference modules. This keeps the primary agent’s tool surface small (which measurably cut module-name guessing) while still giving it the full reference library, figure search, and vision read-off on demand. The behavior is set by reference_mode: 'anytime' (default) offers the consultant always; 'after_calc' only after a calculation has run; 'off' keeps the legacy direct-call behavior.

3.4 Vision: reading drawings and charts

When the engine supports images, the agent gains vision tools: analyze_image and analyze_pdf_page for site plans and report pages, and read_reference_figure, which finds a design chart by meaning (figure_search) and then renders the actual page and reads a value off it — rather than answering a chart value from memory. Attach files before asking:

with open("cross_section.pdf", "rb") as f:
    agent.add_attachment("section", f.read())
result = agent.ask("Extract the slope geometry from 'section' and find the FOS by Bishop.")

# direct geometry extraction (bypasses the ReAct loop)
geo = agent.extract_geometry_from_pdf(pdf_bytes, page=0)
geo.surface_points, geo.boundary_profiles

3.5 The v2 deep agent and notebook chat

The plain install includes funhouse_agent.deep.build_deep_agent, a deepagents/LangGraph-based loop with the same toolbox and an optional staged, human-gated model-setup sub-agent (off by default). For interactive use in Jupyter or Databricks, NotebookChat (v1) and DeepNotebookChat (v2) give an ipywidgets chat with file upload, collapsible tool calls, and inline calc-package preview:

from funhouse_agent.notebook import NotebookChat
chat = NotebookChat(agent)
chat.display()
chat.attach("/Volumes/proj/site_plan.png")   # or the upload widget
Treat agent output as a first draft

The agent can select the wrong method, mis-transcribe a value, or read a chart imperfectly. Run it with verbose=True or an on_tool_call callback so you can see every method and parameter it used, and review the tool calls — not just the prose — before relying on anything.

4.1 Shallow foundations

Sizing and checking spread footings and mats: how much load the ground carries, and how far it settles.

4.1.1 bearing_capacity — Bearing capacity

Problems it solves

Sizing a spread footing or mat and confirming the ground can carry it: the ultimate bearing capacity, the allowable pressure at a chosen factor of safety, and the sensitivity of both to width, embedment, groundwater, eccentricity, and a layered profile.

Methods & theories implemented
  • General bearing-capacity equation with one of two correction-factor sets: Vesic (default; GEC-6 Eq. 5-7, shape factors Table 5-2) or Meyerhof (1963; UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-6). Nγ is the set’s own, 2(Nq+1)tan φ (GEC-6 Eq. 5-8) or (Nq−1)tan(1.4φ), or Brinch Hansen’s 1.5(Nq−1)tan φ (UFC Table 5-2) when named.
  • Terzaghi bearing capacity (general or local shear) with the UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-5 shape factors and no depth or inclination factors (inclined loads, slopes and tilted bases are refused, UFC Table 5-3); Nγ after Kumbhojkar (1993) as tabulated in Das by default, or Coduto et al. (2016), the basis of UFC Table 5-2, each named in the result.
  • Correction factors multiplied (UFC 3-220-20 Eqs. 5-18 to 5-20; GEC-6 Eq. 5-14): shape (GEC-6 Table 5-2); depth by Brinch Hansen’s k (UFC Table 5-8, the default), GEC-6’s dq (Table 5-4) or none (depth_factor_method); load inclination (Vesic, EN 1997-1 Annex D.4); base tilt (GEC-6 Table 5-5); ground slope (Vesic 1975). At φ = 0 the Vesic set adds dc = 0.4k, as UFC Eq. 5-21 does. The Meyerhof set refuses a base tilt or ground slope (UFC Table 5-3; p. 292).
  • Eccentric loading via the Meyerhof effective-area (B′, L′) reduction.
  • Two-layer bearing: a stronger layer over a weaker one by 2V:1H load spread to the weak layer (NAVFAC DM-7.01 ch. 4; Bowles Sec. 4-7); a weaker layer over a stronger one as a bounded transition between the two single-layer capacities, an estimate, not a closed-form solution.
  • Groundwater in the failure wedge through an effective-unit-weight model.
  • References: FHWA GEC-6 (FHWA-SA-02-054) ch. 5; UFC 3-220-20 ch. 5 (Tables 5-2 to 5-8); EN 1997-1 Annex D; Terzaghi (1943); Meyerhof (1963); Brinch Hansen (1970); Vesic (1975).
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Bearing Capacity
MethodWhat it doesParams
bearing_capacity_analysisFull bearing capacity analysis for a shallow foundation (Vesic/Meyerhof/Hansen, or Terzaghi 1943 via factor_method='terzaghi').25
bearing_capacity_factorsQuick lookup of Nc, Nq, Ngamma for a given friction angle (Vesic/Meyerhof/Hansen N-gamma, or Terzaghi's factors).4

layer1_thicknessfloatoptionalFirst layer thickness (m) for 2-layer.

factor_methodstroptionalShape/depth/inclination-factor method. Each takes its own N-gamma unless ngamma_method names another; 'meyerhof' = UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-6, with the shape factors 1 under an inclined load (its note A); it has no base-tilt or ground-slope factors (UFC p. 294, Table 5-3), so base_tilt and ground_slope are refused with it. Hansen applies to N-gamma only: use ngamma_method='hansen'. 'terzaghi' = Terzaghi (1943): his Nc, Nq, N-gamma and shape coefficients (1.3cNc; 0.4/0.3 gamma B Ngamma square/circular), no depth or inclination factors; not for inclined loads, slopes or tilted bases (UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-3). allowed: vesic, meyerhof, terzaghi default: "vesic"
ngamma_methodstroptionalNgamma factor method. Default depends on factor_method: the method's own, 'vesic' = 2(Nq+1)tan(phi) (GEC-6 Eq. 5-8), 'meyerhof' = (Nq-1)tan(1.4 phi) (UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-6), 'kumbhojkar' with factor_method='terzaghi'. 'hansen' = 1.5(Nq-1)tan(phi). Another than the method's own is a mixed method; the result's choices say so. With factor_method='terzaghi' (Terzaghi gave N-gamma only as a chart): 'kumbhojkar' (Kumbhojkar 1993 as tabulated in Das) or 'coduto' (Coduto et al. 2016 approximation, UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-2); the result reports the other beside it. allowed: vesic, meyerhof, hansen, kumbhojkar, coduto
failure_modestroptionalfactor_method='terzaghi' only: 'local' applies Terzaghi's local-shear reduction c* = 2/3 c, tan(phi*) = 2/3 tan(phi) (UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-4). allowed: general, local default: "general"
base_tiltfloatoptionalBase tilt angle (degrees). With factor_method 'vesic' only (GEC-6 Table 5-5 factors); 'meyerhof' and 'terzaghi' have none and refuse it (UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-3). default: 0.0
eccentricity_BfloatoptionalLoad eccentricity along B (m). default: 0.0
eccentricity_LfloatoptionalLoad eccentricity along L (m). default: 0.0
load_inclinationfloatoptionalLoad inclination from vertical (degrees), 0 to below 90; with factor_method 'meyerhof' below phi, as UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-6 takes theta = atan(H/V) < phi' (refused at phi or more). default: 0.0
ground_slopefloatoptionalGround slope angle down from horizontal (degrees), 0 to 45, this tool's own limit: Vesic's g_q = (1 - tan omega)^2 is 0 at 45 deg. With factor_method 'vesic' only; 'meyerhof' and 'terzaghi' have no ground-slope factors and refuse it (UFC 3-220-20 p. 294, Table 5-3). For a footing on or near a slope GEC-6 Sec. 5.2.3.4 uses N_cq and N_gamma-q (Fig. 5-7). default: 0.0
vertical_loadfloatoptionalRequired with factor_method 'vesic', a load_inclination and a soil with cohesion (or phi = 0): the vertical load V on the footing (kN; kN/m for a strip). Vesic's load inclination factors take H = V tan(load_inclination) over V + A' c cot(phi) (Vesic 1975, EN 1997-1:2004 Annex D.4); with c = 0 that is tan(load_inclination) and V cancels. Without it the call is refused (factor_method 'meyerhof' takes the angle alone, UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-6).
depth_factor_methodstroptionalDepth factors for an embedded footing. 'hansen': Brinch Hansen's (1970) k = Df/B below Df/B = 1, arctan(Df/B) from 1 (UFC 3-220-20 Tables 5-7, 5-8 note B) in the factor_method's d factors (Meyerhof's: k = Df/B up to 1 as UFC Table 5-6 prints it); at phi = 0 Vesic's cohesion term adds Table 5-7's d_c = 0.4 k, as UFC Eq. 5-21 does. 'gec6' (factor_method 'vesic' only): GEC-6 Eq. 5-14 and Table 5-4, d_q on the surcharge term alone, 1.0 below Df/B = 1. 'linear' (factor_method 'meyerhof' only): Meyerhof's depth factors with k = Df/B at every depth, as UFC Table 5-6 (p. 294) prints them, d_c = 1 + 0.2 k sqrt(Kp), d_q = d_gamma = 1 + 0.1 k sqrt(Kp) for phi > 10 deg (1 at phi = 0); larger than 'hansen' beyond Df/B = 1. 'none': no depth factors, as GEC-6 Sec. 5.2.3.3 advises unless the cover over the footing is competent and sure to stay. The result's choices give what each option gives. allowed: hansen, gec6, linear, none default: "hansen"
Worked example

Ask → A 2 m × 10 m strip footing bears 1.5 m deep in a c–φ soil (φ=30°, c=10 kPa, γ=18 kN/m³), water 5 m down. What is the bearing capacity and the allowable pressure at FOS = 3?

call_agent(
    agent_name='bearing_capacity',
    method='bearing_capacity_analysis',
    parameters={
        "width": 2.0,
        "length": 10.0,
        "depth": 1.5,
        "shape": "rectangular",
        "cohesion": 10.0,
        "friction_angle": 30.0,
        "unit_weight": 18.0,
        "gwt_depth": 5.0,
        "factor_of_safety": 3.0
    },
)

Applicability limits & conventions
  • By default compute() applies Brinch Hansen’s depth factors and averages the effective unit weight over a depth B below the base. This runs higher than an example that takes dq = 1.0 (GEC-6 Table 5-4 note) and GEC-6’s Cwq, Cwγ groundwater factors (Eq. 5-14): +17.6 % on GEC-6 Example B-1 (V-021). depth_factor_method "gec6" or "none" gives the example’s depth factor; Cw is not offered.
  • The Vesic and Meyerhof sets assume general shear. Local shear is offered with Terzaghi’s factors only (c* = 2/3 c, tan φ* = 2/3 tan φ; UFC 3-220-20 Table 5-4). Punching shear (Meyerhof & Hanna 1978) is not modelled.

4.1.2 settlement — Settlement

Problems it solves

How far a foundation settles and how fast: immediate (elastic) movement, primary consolidation of clays, granular settlement of sands, and the settlement–time curve.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Elastic (immediate) settlement with shape/rigidity influence factors.
  • Schmertmann (1978) strain-influence-factor method for granular soils (NHI-06-089 Eqs. 8-16 to 8-18): the diagram interpolated in L/B between the axisymmetric and plane-strain cases, the peak at the effective stress there (gamma_soil required).
  • One-dimensional Cc/Cr e–log p consolidation with layer summation and preconsolidation (NC/OC).
  • Hough (1959) granular C′-index settlement (bearing-capacity index from corrected SPT N′; GEC-6 Fig 5-19).
  • Stress increase by the 2:1 method, Boussinesq, or Westergaard (read off UFS 3-220-10 Fig. 4-10); secondary compression (Cα); Terzaghi time-rate for the settlement–time curve.
  • References: Schmertmann et al. (1978); Hough (1959); Terzaghi 1-D consolidation; FHWA GEC-6.

Applicability limits & conventions
  • The Hough C′ index is the Hough bearing-capacity index, not Cc/(1+e0) — use the consolidation path for cohesive soils and Hough/Schmertmann for granular.

4.2 Deep foundations

Driven piles, drilled shafts, and pile groups — axial capacity, lateral response, drivability, group action, and downdrag.

4.2.1 axial_pile — Axial pile capacity

Problems it solves

Axial capacity of a driven pile in compression (and uplift): the skin friction and toe resistance developed as the pile passes through a layered profile, and how capacity grows with embedment depth.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Nordlund method in cohesionless soils (GEC-12 Sec. 7.2.1.3.1, Eqs. 7-8, 7-9): δ/φ from Fig. 7-9, Kδ from Tables 7-6 and 7-7, CF from Fig. 7-14, αt and N′q from Fig. 7-16; σ′p at the toe limited to 3 ksf (Step 8) and the unit toe resistance to qL from Fig. 7-15 (after Meyerhof 1976).
  • α-method in cohesive soils (GEC-12 Sec. 7.2.1.3.2, Eq. 7-10): the adhesion Ca read off Fig. 7-17 (Tomlinson) by su, pile type and D/b; Fig. 7-18’s stratigraphy cases, or the smaller of the two, on request (p. 246). Past the chart’s curves, API α (Eqs. 7-13, 7-14) in a clay the engineer calls highly overconsolidated, else Ca held at the curve’s end (p. 247). A layer’s own α or Ca, with its basis, replaces the chart. Toe 9·su (Eq. 7-11).
  • β-method (Fellenius 1991; GEC-12 Sec. 7.2.1.3.4, Eqs. 7-19, 7-20) in every layer on request: β and Nt from Table 7-9 by soil type, where a layer gives none (Steps 2b, 5b).
  • Factored resistance (Q_factored) by GEC-12 Eq. 7-3 with Table 7-1’s factors by method (Nordlund 0.45, α-method 0.35; none for the β-method, p. 258), and factored uplift by Eq. 7-38 (0.35 / 0.25 / 0.20). The allowable capacity uses FS 2.5 (NHI-06-089 Table 9-5, indicator piles with wave-equation analysis).
  • Groundwater-split effective-stress integration; optional per-layer separate shaft/toe friction angle; below-grade pile head (head_depth); uplift capacity.
  • Pile sections: closed and open pipe, square and circular concrete, timber, H-piles (box perimeter and toe area, Vol. I pp. 247, 408) and a custom section. An open pipe is the lesser of the plugged and unplugged cases (Eqs. 7-88, 7-89), or Tomlinson’s Eq. 7-90 under 24 in in mainly cohesive soil (Sec. 7.10.7).
  • References: FHWA GEC-12 Vol. I (FHWA-NHI-16-009) ch. 7; validated against GEC-12 Vol. III (FHWA-NHI-16-064) Tables D-6, D-100 and D-51 (V-001, V-002, V-059).

GEC-12 itself designs by resistance factors: the result also gives the factored resistance (Table 7-1, Eq. 7-3). default: 2.5

h_pile_toe_areastroptionalH-pile toe area: 'box' (depth x flange width, GEC-12 Sec. 7.10.7) or 'steel'. GEC-12 Step 9 leaves it to past experience and local load tests. allowed: box, steel default: "box"
adhesion_curvestroptionalalpha-method: GEC-12 Fig. 7-17 curves. 'auto' = smooth steel for pipe piles, the concrete/timber/corrugated curve for H-piles (GEC-12 Vol I p. 247) and concrete or timber piles. allowed: auto, concrete_timber_corrugated, smooth_steel default: "auto"
adhesion_beyond_chartstroptionalalpha method where a clay layer's su is past the end of the chart's curves (Fig. 7-17, or 7-18 where read); GEC-12 Vol I p. 247 and alpha-method Step 1 recommend API RP 2A's alpha there for highly overconsolidated clays. 'api_if_highly_overconsolidated': API alpha in a layer whose su / sigma'vo is at or above highly_overconsolidated_su_ratio, Ca held at the curve's end below it; 'chart_end': Ca held at the curve's end in every such layer (GEC-12's worked example, Vol 3 Table D-100); 'api': API alpha in every such layer. Within the curves Ca is read off Fig. 7-17 as drawn (it can exceed su). allowed: api_if_highly_overconsolidated, chart_end, api default: "api_if_highly_overconsolidated"
highly_overconsolidated_su_ratiofloatoptionalalpha method: the su / sigma'vo at and above which a clay is highly overconsolidated, for adhesion_beyond_chart 'api_if_highly_overconsolidated'. GEC-12 gives no value; it is the engineer's judgment, so a run with a clay layer whose su is past the chart's curves is refused until this (or adhesion_beyond_chart 'chart_end' or 'api') is given. Ask the user, or state the value taken as a judgment call.
displaced_volumefloatoptionalNordlund displaced volume V per unit length (m3/m). Default: the steel area of an H-pile, the gross area of other piles (an open pipe as a closed pipe; its steel area, if it drives unplugged, is below GEC-12 Fig. 7-9).
pile_areafloatoptionalCustom section (m2): the cross-section area, the steel of an H-pile or a closed pipe, the gross area of a concrete or timber pile (it gives the Nordlund displaced volume of an H-pile and of a solid pile). pile_perimeterfloatoptionalCustom section: the perimeter for the side resistance (m); the box perimeter of an H-pile (GEC-12 Steps 6 and Vol I p. 247).
pile_tip_areafloatoptionalCustom section: the toe area (m2). Required for h_pile (its box area; h_pile_toe_area 'steel' takes pile_area) and pipe_closed (the gross area); a concrete or timber pile's is its pile_area when not given.
pile_widthfloatoptionalCustom section: the width or diameter b (m), an H-pile's flange width; for D/b and the width notes.
pile_depthfloatoptionalCustom section: the section's depth (m), an H-pile's; reported only.
pile_namestroptionalCustom section: its name, e.g. 'HP16x101'.

A layer's case is its fig_7_18_case, else from the profile: cohesive layers under a cohesionless layer the sand case, from the ground surface the stiff-clay case; the soft-clay case only where a layer gives it. Eq. 7-90 (open pipe) takes Ca from Fig. 7-17 whatever this is (p. 407). allowed: fig_7_17, fig_7_18, smaller default: "fig_7_17"
shrink_swell_depthfloatoptionalDepth (m below the ground surface) of a shrink-swell zone: no shaft resistance in cohesive soil above it (GEC-12 Vol I p. 247). Default none.
beta_coefficientsstroptionalmethod='beta': beta and Nt where a layer gives none: GEC-12 Table 7-9 by the layer's soil_class (clay 0.15-0.35, silt 0.25-0.50, sand 0.30-0.90, gravel 0.35-0.80; Steps 2b/5b), a straight line in phi' between Table 7-9's range ends (the module's reading; the table prints only the ends). A clay toe takes cohesive_Nt. GEC-12 prints no beta formula from phi' alone; give a layer's beta and Nt for other values (local experience, Steps 2a/5a). allowed: table_7_9 default: "table_7_9"
toe_phi_zonestroptionalNordlund toe: the phi near the toe. 'toe_layer' (the toe layer's toe_friction_angle or friction_angle) or 'average_3b' (averaged over the cohesionless soil from the toe to 3b below, GEC-12 Step 7c's zone). allowed: toe_layer, average_3b default: "toe_layer"

Applicability limits & conventions
  • With the choices GEC-12’s South Abutment example made (Vol. III Table D-100: adhesion_curve="smooth_steel", adhesion_beyond_chart="chart_end") the shaft is within 1 % of the print (V-002). The defaults take Fig. 7-17’s corrugated curve for an H-pile (Vol. I p. 247) and read 13–14 % higher.
  • Where a clay’s su is past Fig. 7-17’s curves, GEC-12 takes API α for highly overconsolidated clay but prints no su/σ′vo that marks one (p. 247; Step 1, p. 250). The run is refused until highly_overconsolidated_su_ratio or the layer’s highly_overconsolidated is given.
  • Datum matters: reference the profile to the pile head (e.g. a below-grade footing) so no spurious skin friction is added above the head.

4.2.2 lateral_pile — Lateral pile analysis

Problems it solves

Lateral response of a pile or drilled shaft under head shear, moment, and axial load: deflection, rotation, bending-moment, shear, and soil-reaction profiles with depth, for free or fixed heads and above-ground stickup.

Methods & theories implemented
  • p–y curve soil models (COM624P / LPILE family): Matlock soft clay, Reese stiff clay above/below water table, Reese (1974) sand (GEC 9's four-segment construction by default, a simplified one on request), API sand, and others.
  • Banded finite-difference beam-column solver with P-Δ (axial-load) effects.
  • Free/fixed head conditions, above-ground stickup, and H-pile strong/weak-axis or concrete-filled-pipe sections.
  • References: FHWA GEC 9 (FHWA-HIF-18-031) App. A; Reese, Cox & Koop (1974); Matlock (1970); COM624P; validated against GEC 9 Example B.1, a COM624P oracle suite and the FHWA Micropile LPILE benchmark (V-017).

(1975), stiff clay with free water: GEC 9 p. 219 keeps it for stiff clay exposed to free water at or near the ground surface, and with the groundwater at depth prefers StiffClayAboveWT (Welch & Reese) even below the water table, gamma then submerged; it does not say how near is near, so which of the two a stiff clay below the water table takes is the engineer's call: state it and why, or ask; SoftClayJeanjean {su, gamma, Gmax} (not checked against a print: neither Jeanjean 2009 nor API RP 2GEO is in the reference library; GEC 9's soft clay criterion is SoftClayMatlock); SandReese/SandAPI {phi, gamma, k} where k (kN/m3) is the k of the initial line p = (k z) y: for SandReese GEC 9 Table A-3 gives it by relative density only, loose / medium / dense 5,429 / 16,287 / 33,931 submerged and 6,786 / 24,430 / 61,076 above the water (20 / 60 / 125 and 25 / 90 / 225 lb/in3); for SandAPI API RP 2A Fig. 6.8.7-1 by phi', e.g. phi' 30 / 35 / 40: 9,260 / 22,260 / 42,510 below the water table and 12,650 / 36,970 / 75,270 above; WeakRock {qu, Er}. SandReese also takes optional construction='reese1974' (default: GEC 9 App. A.4's four-segment curve, linear -> parabola -> straight line -> p_u, A and B from Figs. A-10 and A-11) | 'simplified' (the module's own three-part curve, which no held page prints). StiffClayAboveWT with loading='cyclic' also needs n_cycles, N, the number of times the design lateral load is applied (>= 1; the references give no number to assume; Welch & Reese, COM624P Eq. 3.29, y_c = y_s + y50 C log N, so y50 times 1 + 0.6 log10 N). WeakRock (Reese 1997, FHWA GEC 9 App. A.5) also takes optional RQD (%, default 100: alpha_r = 1/3, the printed lower bound; alpha_r rises linearly to 1.0 at RQD 0), krm (default 0.0005, the softer end of 0.00005-0.0005) and rock_top (depth of the rock surface, m; default the top of the weak-rock layers that hold the layer); its gamma_r is accepted and not used (the criterion does not use the unit weight).

tolerancefloatoptionalConvergence tolerance on deflection (m). default: 1e-05

Applicability limits & conventions
  • Section stiffness is a linear EI (an uncracked composite section by transformed section) or Branson's cracked EI for reinforced concrete; no moment–curvature analysis. In the micropile benchmark (V-017) the uncracked composite EI gives 3.32 mm against LPILE's 3.3 mm.

4.2.3 pile_group — Pile groups

Problems it solves

How a rigid pile cap distributes structural loads to the individual piles, and how much a group settles: axial/lateral/torsional load sharing under a 6-DOF load set, group efficiency, and group settlement.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Rigid-cap 6-DOF stiffness analysis — per-pile axial and lateral stiffness, batter, and one right-hand sign convention carried end to end.
  • Group efficiency factor ηg read from the printed rows by soil, the cap's contact with the ground and the spacing (GEC-12 Sec. 7.2.2; UFC 3-220-20 Table 6-26 for drilled shafts, CFA, displacement piles and micropiles); block failure by GEC-12 Eqs. 7-36 and 7-37; lateral p-multipliers by row (AASHTO as GEC-12 prints it, or Mokwa, UFC 3-220-20 Table 6-38).
  • Group uplift (GEC-12 Sec. 7.2.3.2; UFC 3-220-20 Eqs. 6-40 to 6-43): the lesser of the piles’ factored tension resistances and the block’s (the group_uplift tool; the rigid-cap tools flag every pile in tension and say to run it, and the pile-group calc package checks the piles in tension when it has the block’s inputs).
  • Meyerhof (1976) SPT group settlement as GEC-12 Eqs. 7-50 to 7-52 print it, and an elastic equivalent-footing settlement (GEC-12 Sec. 7.3.5.3, Eq. 7-55, 2V:1H spread) summed to where the stress falls to 10 % of the footing’s bearing stress (UFC 3-220-20 p. 449; GEC-12 step 1c’s 10 % of the existing effective stress as influence_depth_m).
  • References: FHWA GEC-12 Vol. I ch. 7; UFC 3-220-20 ch. 6; validated against GEC-12 Vol. III Tables D-13, D-14 and D-23 and UFC 3-220-20 Appendix B-5.4 (V-005, V-060).
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)
Pile Group
MethodWhat it doesParams

group_upliftUplift resistance of a pile group in net tension, or of the piles in tension of a group (GEC-12 Vol. III checks the back row in tension of an abutment group in compression), as GEC-12 Sec. 7.2.3.2 and UFC 3-220-20 Eqs. 6-40 to 6-43 print it: the lesser of the sum of the piles' factored tension resistances and the group's as a block (cohesionless soil: the effective weight of the soil within sides at 1H:4V from the toes; cohesive soil: the block's weight plus 2D(B+Z)su on its sides), factored by phi_ug.16

Applicability limits & conventions

4.2.4 drilled_shaft — Drilled shafts

Problems it solves

Axial capacity of a drilled shaft (bored pile) in soil and rock: side resistance in clay and sand, base resistance, rock-socket capacity, belled bases, and the LRFD factored resistance.

Methods & theories implemented
  • α-method side resistance in clay (GEC-10 (2018) Eq. 10-18 rational α by default, on su(CIUC): cu is taken as su(CIUC) unless su_test_type says it came from a UU or UC test, when Eqs. 10-16/10-17 transform it; the O’Neill & Reese (1999) AASHTO α by name).
  • β-method side resistance in sand (GEC-10 (2018) Eq. 10-13 by default: Ko from the OCR, σ′p from each layer’s N60; or the O’Neill–Reese depth β by name).
  • Base resistance in sand (GEC-10 Eq. 10-14 on the mean N60 over two diameters below the base) and clay (N*c·su, Eq. 10-19, su averaged over two diameters); no large-base reduction unless asked for, as the 2018 edition prints none.
  • Rock sockets: side resistance by Eq. 10-21 with C = 1.0 by default (rock_side_C; GEC-10 gives 0.65, Eq. 10-22’s value at αE = 1, and 1.9 for roughened sockets, a C above 1.0 to be verified by load tests or local experience; Eq. 10-22 for caving sockets), qu held no higher than the concrete’s f′c when it is given; base 2.5 qu (Eq. 10-23) only where the engineer states the conditions of p. 10-22 or the rock below the base is at RQD 100 (a rock layer given no RQD is taken at 100, so a profile without RQD gets 2.5 qu, and the result’s choices say so), else the Hoek–Brown base or a refusal. Permanent casing, fractured rock at the top of the socket, and a top exclusion zone in clay (1.5 m by default; none in sand or rock unless given).
  • LRFD resistance factors and capacity-vs-depth curves.
  • References: FHWA GEC-10 (FHWA-NHI-18-024); O’Neill & Reese; Chen & Kulhawy; validated against the GEC-10 Appendix A example (V-006/V-007/V-008).

GSI or m_i on any other layer (above the base, further below it, or with the base in soil) is refused: nothing would use them; capacity_vs_depth takes them on any layer a trial base is in.

'rqd' = q_b/q_u reduced by the tip rock's RQD below 70 (1.5 at 50, 0.8 at 25, 0.4 at 0), cited to GEC-10's 2010 edition, not in the reference library, and not a method GEC-10 Table 8-4 gives a resistance factor for. allowed: gec10, rqd default: "gec10"

The engineer's judgment: Example 10-4 takes 2.5 with RQD 37 to 100 because 'Rock coring and local experience indicate the rock mass below the socket tip is competent'. true = 2.5*qu (Eq. 10-23) as stated. false = GEC-10's base for a fractured rock mass, the Hoek-Brown base (Eqs. 10-24 to 10-29), on the tip rock layer's GSI and m_i; refused, naming them, where that layer does not give them. Left out = taken as met, said in the result's choices, where every layer within one base diameter below the base is rock with RQD 100 (the layer default), with the Hoek-Brown base on the tip rock layer's GSI and m_i beside it where they are given; where a layer there has an RQD below 100 or is soil, the Hoek-Brown base on the tip rock layer's GSI and m_i (2.5*qu bounds it above), and the call is refused, naming them, where that layer does not give them.

Default false: GEC-10 (2018) prints neither (Eqs. 10-14, 10-19, 10-20); true applies it. default: false
pafloatoptionalAtmospheric pressure (kPa) for the rational chains. default: 101.325
rock_side_CfloatoptionalC in the rock side resistance f_s = C*pa*sqrt(qu/pa) (GEC-10 Eq. 10-21, p. 10-20). For rock_side_method 'normal'; refused with 'caving', which takes no C. Needs a rock layer. default: 1.0
rock_side_methodstroptionalRock side resistance. 'normal' (default) = GEC-10 Eq. 10-21, f_s = C*pa*sqrt(qu/pa) with rock_side_C, for a 'normal' socket: conventional equipment, nominally clean sidewalls (pp. 10-20, 10-21). 'caving' = Eq. 10-22 (O'Neill and Reese 1999), f_s = 0.65*alpha_E*pa*sqrt(qu/pa), alpha_E from Table 10-3 (p. 10-21) by each rock layer's RQD and rock_joints (closed joints 1.00, 0.85, 0.60, 0.50, 0.45; open or gouge-filled 0.85, 0.55, 0.55, 0.50, 0.45 at RQD 100, 70, 50, 30, 20 %; linear between the rows, held at 0.45 below RQD 20), for highly fractured or weathered rock that cannot be drilled without artificial support (casing, plug-ahead) or where caving is anticipated. One diameter for every rock layer: GEC-10 sizes a socket by one diameter B (Eq. 10-3, p. 10-9; Example 10-4) and gives none per rock layer. The rock side resistance and, with the tip in rock, the base (pi/4*B^2, GEC-10 Example 10-4, p. 10-28) take it.
bell_diameterfloatoptionalBelled base diameter (m).
casing_depthfloatoptionalPermanent casing depth (m, no side resistance). default: 0.0
fractured_rock_thicknessfloatoptionalDecomposed or fractured rock (m) below the top of the first rock layer that is 'not considered part of the socket for design purposes' (GEC-10 p. 8-15): no rock side resistance over it, while the soil above keeps its own (casing_depth takes both). 0 = all rock is socket. Needs a rock layer. default: 0.0
concrete_fcfloatoptionalCompressive strength f'c of the shaft concrete (kPa; 28 MPa = 28000, at least 1000). The rock side resistance takes qu no higher than it: 'For design, the value of qu used in Equation 10-21 should not exceed the compressive strength of the drilled shaft concrete' (GEC-10 p. 10-21; Example 10-4 gives qu 360 ksf and f'c 576 ksf), in Eq. 10-22 alike. With the base in rock it also checks the base against the concrete's own bearing (GEC-10 p. 10-25): Eq. 12-7 (p. 12-8), 0.70*[0.85*f'c*A1*m], the tip taken as plain concrete as Example 10-4 does (with the cage to the tip p. 12-8 prints Eq. 12-6 at phi 0.70, not computed: the tool takes no f_y), A1 the socket's cross-sectional area, m = 2.0 (printed for a socket on competent rock), against the geotechnical 0.50*Q_tip (Example 10-4 p. 10-28 makes this check), in base_steps.concrete_bearing and the choices; lrfd_capacity takes the factored base as the smaller of the two. Q_tip, Q_ultimate and Q_allowable stay the geotechnical ones. Left out, neither limit is checked and the result's choices say so. No other structural check of the shaft is made. Needs a rock layer.

Applicability limits & conventions
  • The O’Neill & Reese large-base reduction is off by default (large_base_reduction), because GEC-10 (2018) prints none; an example worked to the 2010 edition or to NHI-06-089 with the reduction will differ by that factor.

4.2.5 wave_equation — Wave-equation drivability

Problems it solves

Pile drivability and the dynamic bearing check: the bearing graph (static resistance vs blow count), driving stresses, and refusal, from a hammer–cushion–pile–soil model — the analysis behind a driven-pile field acceptance criterion.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Smith (1960) one-dimensional wave-equation model: the pile as lumped masses and springs about 1 m long (GEC-12 Vol. 2 p. 155), elasto-plastic soil springs (quake) with smith or smith-viscous damping (UFC 3-220-20 p. 488), one cushion spring with the helmet’s mass lumped with the first pile segment, and explicit central-difference time integration.
  • Single-blow analysis, bearing graph, and drivability vs depth: one pile in the leads, embedded to each depth (embedded_length; GEC-12 Vol. 2 pp. 224, 227). The permanent set is the maximum toe displacement less the quakes (p. 158). Refusal is at 120 blows/ft by default (p. 161). Fourteen built-in hammers take the ram weights, strokes and energies of Vol. 2 Appendix C; custom ram, stroke and efficiency are accepted. With no cushion given, only the Vulcan 014 takes Table 12-2’s cushion and helmet (p. 183); any other hammer needs the cushion, its COR and the helmet weight.
  • References: Smith (1960); GRLWEAP-style modelling; FHWA GEC-12.

R_minfloatoptionalMin resistance (kN). default: 200.0
R_maxfloatoptionalMax resistance (kN). default: 2000.0
R_stepfloatoptionalResistance increment (kN). default: 200.0
skin_fractionfloatoptionalSkin friction fraction. default: 0.5
damping_modelstroptionalSmith damping form (UFC 3-220-20 (2025) Sec. 6-9.2, pp. 487-488): 'smith' (default), damping proportional to the mobilized static resistance, J x R_static x v, set 'in most instances' (GEC-12 Vol 2 p. 242); 'smith_viscous', proportional to the fully mobilized static resistance, J x R_ult x v, which GEC-12 Vol 2 (p. 242) selects for a residual stress analysis or a vibratory hammer, and sometimes for a refined analysis's match. allowed: smith, smith_viscous default: "smith"
quake_sidefloatoptionalShaft quake (m): 0.10 in (0.0025 m), usually satisfactory (GEC-12 Vol 2 Sec. 12.6.7, p. 211). default: 0.0025
quake_toefloatoptionalToe quake (m). Default 0.10 in (0.0025 m), GEC-12 Vol 2's toe quake for a non-displacement pile, e.g. an H-pile (p. 171). A displacement pile (closed end pipe, concrete): pile diameter or width D over 120 to D over 60 (p. 211), D/60 in medium or dense sand and D/120 in very dense soil (Examples 1, 3, 6, pp. 162, 170, 182); GEC-12 Vol 3 (p. 40) also gives H-piles D/60 and D/120. Hard rock: 0.04 in (0.001 m) (p. 212). Saturated or sensitive soils can reach well over D/60 (p. 211). default: 0.0025
damping_sidefloatoptionalShaft Smith damping (s/m), GEC-12 Vol 2 Sec. 12.6.7 (p. 211): 0.05 s/ft (0.16 s/m, the default) non-cohesive soils, 0.10 s/ft (0.33) silty sands, clayey sands and sandy silts, 0.15 s/ft (0.49) cohesive silts and sandy clays, 0.20 s/ft (0.66) cohesive soils. For restrike, perhaps twice as high (p. 211). default: 0.16
damping_toefloatoptionalToe Smith damping (s/m): about 0.15 s/ft (0.49 s/m) for most soils (GEC-12 Vol 2 p. 211); lower on hard rock, e.g. 0.05 s/ft (0.16 s/m) (p. 212). default: 0.49
embedded_lengthfloatoptionalThe pile's embedded length, its penetration below grade (m), at most pile_length: the shaft resistance acts only below grade, the pile above it standing free (GEC-12 Vol 2 p. 224: 'Penetration refers to the analyzed pile toe penetration below grade'; Example 1, p. 162, a 65 ft pile driven 62 ft; Example 6, p. 182, 66 ft with 'an embedded length of 52.5 feet'). Left out: pile_length, the pile embedded over its full length.
shaft_distributionstroptionalHow the shaft resistance (skin_fraction of R_ult) is spread over the embedded length, as GEC-12 Vol 2's examples print it: 'uniform' (default), the same per metre (Example 5, p. 179: '92% uniform shaft resistance'); 'triangular', rising linearly from none at grade to its largest at the pile toe (Example 1, p. 162, Fig. 12-3; Example 6, p. 182: 'distributed triangularly along the embedded portion of the pile shaft'). A distribution from a static analysis layer by layer (Example 4, Fig. 12-9) is not offered. GEC-12 Vol 2 p. 212: the stresses, tension above all, are sensitive to the distribution. allowed: uniform, triangular default: "uniform"
ram_weightfloatoptionalCustom hammer ram weight (kN) — used with stroke when hammer_name is omitted.
strokefloatoptionalCustom hammer stroke (m).
efficiencyfloatoptionalCustom hammer efficiency: the share of the potential ram energy (ram weight x stroke) that reaches the ram as kinetic energy at impact (GEC-12 Vol 2 (FHWA-NHI-16-010) Sec. 12.6.2, p. 205). GEC-12 Vol 2 prints 0.67 for an air hammer and 0.80 for an open end diesel (Example 6, p. 185), and say 0.95 for a hydraulic hammer whose ram kinetic energy is measured (p. 205). Default 0.67. default: 0.67
hammer_custom_namestroptionalCustom hammer label. default: "Custom"
hammer_typestroptionalCustom hammer type: a label in the result and calc package only. Every type is modelled as a rigid ram striking at v = sqrt(2 g stroke efficiency); a diesel hammer's combustion pressure is not modelled, and its result carries a warning (GEC-12 Vol 2 p. 206: its stroke rises with the resistance, and too high a stroke gives non-conservative nominal resistances). Give the type's losses through efficiency (GEC-12 Vol 2 (FHWA-NHI-16-010) Sec. 12.6.2, p. 205: relatively high, say 0.95, for a hydraulic hammer whose ram kinetic energy is measured and displayed). allowed: single_acting, diesel, hydraulic default: "single_acting"
segment_lengthfloatoptionalPile segment length (m): about 1 m (GEC-12 Vol 2 Sec. 12.3, p. 155; GRLWEAP's 3.3 ft, p. 213). Shorter segments for stiff, uncushioned driving systems (p. 210). default: 1.0
cushion_stiffnessfloatoptionalHammer cushion stiffness (kN/m), with cushion_cor and helmet_weight. Or give cushion_area + cushion_thickness + cushion_E: stiffness = E A / t (GEC-12 Vol 2 p. 155); two materials in series 1/k = 1/k1 + 1/k2 (p. 209). The model has one cushion spring, between the ram and the helmet (whose weight is lumped with the pile head); GEC-12 Vol 2 Fig. 12-2 (p. 157) has a hammer cushion and a pile cushion with the helmet between. Left out with no cushion properties: the hammer's printed driving system where a held reference prints one (hammer_name 'Vulcan 014', GEC-12 Vol 2 Table 12-2, p. 183), or the one named by driving_system; for any other hammer the call is refused and the error lists the printed options (GEC-12 prints no cushion by hammer otherwise; ideally the contractor's submittal, Vol II p. 226).
cushion_areafloatoptionalCushion area (m2) — with cushion_thickness and cushion_E.
cushion_thicknessfloatoptionalCushion thickness (m).
cushion_EfloatoptionalCushion elastic modulus (kPa), with the nominal (uncompressed) thickness. Plywood pile cushions 30 ksi (207,000 kPa) new and 75 ksi (517,000 kPa) used; oak boards 60 and 90 ksi (GEC-12 Vol 2 p. 209).
cushion_corfloatoptionalHammer cushion coefficient of restitution, required with a cushion given by stiffness or properties (no held reference prints one COR for every cushion). GEC-12 Vol 2: the hammer cushions of its examples 0.90 to 0.92 (pp. 174, 183); wood 0.50, a badly worn softwood cushion 0.25 (p. 156); a refined analysis adjusts it between 0.10 and 1.0 (p. 216). With a printed driving system and no cushion given: that system's COR unless given (Vulcan 014 0.91, ICE 42S 0.92, p. 183).
pile_EfloatoptionalPile elastic modulus (kPa). Default steel, 29,000 ksi (GEC-12 Vol 1 p. 317). Concrete: on the order of 4,000 ksi, varying with its strength (Vol 1 p. 317); its dynamic modulus is usually higher than the static (Vol 2 p. 213). default: 200000000.0
pile_unit_weightfloatoptionalPile material unit weight (kN/m3). Default steel, 492 lb/ft3 (GEC-12 Vol 2 p. 462). default: 77.3
helmet_weightfloatoptionalHelmet weight (kN): helmet, hammer cushion, striker plate and inserts (GEC-12 Vol 2 p. 226), lumped with the pile head; 0 with no helmet mass. Required with a cushion given. With a printed driving system and no cushion given: that system's helmet unless given (Vulcan 014 1.67 kips, 7.43 kN; ICE 42S 2.05 kips, 9.12 kN; p. 183). GEC-12's examples give 1.0 to 4.07 kips (4.4 to 18.1 kN; Vol II pp. 163, 167, 174, 179, 183).
driving_systemstroptionalA driving system (hammer cushion and helmet) as a held reference prints it, by its hammer: GEC-12 Vol 2 Example 6, Table 12-2 (p. 183), on a steel pipe pile. 'Vulcan 014': Nycast, 208 ksi, 234 in2, 6.0 in (1.42 million kN/m), COR 0.91, helmet 1.67 kips; 'ICE 42S': Blue Nylon, 175 ksi, 398 in2, 2.0 in (6.10 million kN/m), COR 0.92, helmet 2.05 kips. cushion_cor and helmet_weight, if given, replace the system's. Not with cushion_stiffness or cushion properties. Left out: the named hammer's own printed system, which only hammer_name 'Vulcan 014' has; any other hammer needs a cushion given. A run with another hammer says so in its choices. allowed: ICE 42S, Vulcan 014
Worked example

Ask → For a 20 m steel pile driven by a Vulcan 014 hammer, plot the bearing graph — blows per metre against static resistance.

call_agent(
    agent_name='wave_equation',
    method='bearing_graph',
    parameters={
        "pile_length": 20.0,
        "pile_area": 0.012,
        "hammer_name": "Vulcan 014",
        "R_min": 500.0,
        "R_max": 3000.0,
        "R_step": 500.0
    },
)
Representative output (real, from the shipped code)
R_values_kN: [6 entries]
blow_counts_per_m: [6 entries]
permanent_sets_m: [6 entries]
max_comp_stresses_kPa: [6 entries]
max_tens_stresses_kPa: [6 entries]
choices: [1 entries]
defaults_used: {skin_fraction=0.5, damping_model=smith, quake_side=0.0025, quake_toe=0.0025, damping_side=0.16, damping_toe=0.49}

With no cushion given, the Vulcan 014 takes its hammer cushion and helmet as GEC-12 Vol 2 Table 12-2 prints them (p. 183); any other hammer needs the cushion, its COR and the helmet weight given, or driving_system.

Applicability limits & conventions
  • Every hammer is a rigid ram striking at v = √(2ghη) (GEC-12 Vol. 2 Eq. 15-1). A diesel’s combustion and changing stroke are not modelled, and the result warns that its blow counts are likely low (p. 206). Treat a diesel bearing graph as a trend, not a tie-out (V-003: 48 against the published 120 blows/ft; GEC-12 Example 6, ICE 42-S: 50 and 103 against 99 and 209).

4.2.6 downdrag — Downdrag / neutral plane

Problems it solves

Negative skin friction (downdrag) on a pile through settling ground: the neutral plane, the maximum axial load in the pile, and the drag load added to the structural load.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Neutral plane method — every method the references give, side by side with its neutral plane, drag force and settlement: the intersection of the load and resistance curves at 100 / 50 / 0 % toe mobilization (UFC 3-220-20 §6-7.4, §6-5.8.4.2; GEC-12 §7.3.6.1), the toe resistance compatible with the toe penetration (UFC §6-5.8.4.3), the neutral plane at the bearing layer or at the pile toe, and Endo et al. (1969). The headline is UFC 3-220-20’s §6-7.4 procedure; skin friction on the final effective stress.
  • Fill-induced downdrag, groundwater drawdown, and a maximum-load structural check.
  • The toe’s Nt from GEC-12 Table 7-9 (UFC Table 6-17, Fellenius) by soil type, or Cheng (2004) by name; 9·su in clay. The pile’s weight is left out of the load curve, as UFC Fig. 6-26 and GEC-12 §7.3.6.1 do (include_pile_weight). The toe load is counted below the toe to 10 % of the equivalent footing’s bearing stress (UFC §6-5.8.4.3), or GEC-12’s 10 % of the effective stress on request.
  • References: UFC 3-220-20; FHWA GEC-12; Fellenius; CGPR #56; validated against GEC-12 (V-004, NP/Qmax/DF within 0.2%) and UFC App. B-5.5.
Agent-callable methods (from the shipped registry)

Parameters of downdrag_analysis
ParameterTypeDescription
pile_lengthfloatrequiredPile length (m).
pile_diameterfloatrequiredPile diameter (m).
layersarrayrequiredArray of {thickness, soil_type, unit_weight, phi, cu, beta, alpha, skin_friction_method, soil_class, settling, description} dicts. soil_type must be 'cohesionless' or 'cohesive' (NOT 'sand'/'clay'/'settling_fill'). Skin friction: cohesionless = beta x sigma'v (Beta method, UFC 3-220-20 Eq 6-7), beta as given, else from phi' by GEC-12 Table 7-9 (UFC 3-220-20 Table 6-15, driven piles) for the layer's soil_class ('silt' 0.25-0.50 over 28-34 deg, 'sand' 0.30-0.90 over 32-40 deg, the default, 'gravel' 0.35-0.80 over 35-45 deg), a straight line in phi' between GEC-12 Table 7-9's range ends (the module's reading; the table prints only the ends), held at the ends outside the range; soil_class also picks the toe's Nt row (Nt_method); cohesive = alpha x cu (Alpha method, UFC 3-220-20 Eq 6-8, the default; alpha as given, else read off alpha_chart: UFC 3-220-20 Table 6-16 and Fig 6-14 by default), or with skin_friction_method 'beta' beta x sigma'v for long-term, drained conditions (UFC 3-220-20 6-5.4.1; GEC-12 7.2.1.3.4), beta required (GEC-12 Table 7-9: clay 0.15-0.35; cu then only for a toe in the layer). A cohesive layer takes no phi, and beta only with skin_friction_method 'beta'; a cohesionless layer takes no alpha. Mark settling layers with settling=True; a settling layer also needs its compressibility: cohesionless -> E_s (elastic modulus, kPa, > 0) and optional nu_s; cohesive -> Cc and e0 (optional Cr, sigma_p kPa) or C_ec/C_er.

fill_thicknessfloatoptionalFill thickness causing downdrag (m). default: 0.0
fill_unit_weightfloatoptionalFill unit weight (kN/m3). default: 19.0
gw_drawdownfloatoptionalGroundwater drawdown (m). default: 0.0
gwt_depthfloatoptionalGroundwater depth (m). default: 0.0
pile_EfloatoptionalPile elastic modulus (kPa). Default is steel. default: 200000000.0
pile_perimeterfloatoptionalPile perimeter (m). Computed from diameter if omitted.
pile_areafloatoptionalPile cross-section area (m2). Computed from diameter if omitted.
structural_capacityfloatoptionalPile structural capacity (kN) for the max-load check.
allowable_settlementfloatoptionalAllowable pile settlement (m) for the settlement check.
NtfloatoptionalToe bearing capacity factor: R_toe = Nt x sigma'v(toe) x A_toe in cohesionless soil, Nt x cu x A_toe in cohesive. Give the MOBILIZED value -- the toe resistance actually developed at the pile's settlement -- not the ultimate. Omitted, Nt is the ULTIMATE value: 9 in clay (UFC 3-220-20 6-5.4.3.3), and in cohesionless soil from the toe layer's phi' by Nt_method (60-120 in dense sand at 34-38 deg by the default); then the load and resistance curves often do not intersect and the neutral plane is where the pile and soil settle equally, the toe force compatible with the toe penetration (UFC 3-220-20 6-5.8.4.3; see neutral_plane_method). UFC 3-220-20 6-5.8.4.2: check 0 %, 50 % and 100 % toe mobilization.
Nt_methodstringoptionalWhere a cohesionless toe's ultimate Nt comes from when Nt is not given, both UFC 3-220-20 Table 6-17 (p. 421; qb = Nq sigma'zD, Eq 6-20): 'fellenius' (default) = its Fellenius (2021) column, the same values as GEC-12 Table 7-9, by the toe layer's soil_class (silt 20-40 over 28-34 deg, sand 30-150 over 32-40 deg, gravel 60-300 over 35-45 deg), a straight line in phi' between GEC-12 Table 7-9's range ends (the module's reading; the table prints only the ends), held at the ends outside the range; 'cheng' = its equation after Cheng (2004), Nq ~= 1.2 (Z/b)^-0.437 exp[6.34 (Z/b)^0.0486 tan phi'], Z the pile length and b pile_diameter, at most 200 unless project-specific information supports more (give Nt then). The result's choices give the other route's value. allowed: fellenius, cheng default: "fellenius"
pile_unit_weightfloatoptionalPile material unit weight (kN/m3), times pile_area for the pile's own weight; used only when include_pile_weight is true. Default 78.5 = steel, the same material as the pile_E default (concrete is about 24). For an H or pipe pile give pile_area as the steel area (pile_area defaults to the solid circle). default: 78.5
include_pile_weightbooloptionalWhether the load curve carries the pile's own weight. Default false: left out, as UFC 3-220-20 Fig 6-26 and FHWA GEC-12 7.3.6.1 (and their worked examples) do. True adds the weight of the pile above the neutral plane to Q_np and the drag force. default: false
n_sublayersintoptionalSublayers per soil layer for the depth discretization. default: 10
neutral_plane_methodstringoptionalWhich method gives the reported numbers; every method is evaluated and returned in neutral_plane_comparison whatever is chosen. 'auto' (default) = the UFC 3-220-20 6-7.4 procedure: the intersection of the load and resistance curves with the toe at toe_mobilization, or, when they do not intersect, where the pile and soil settle equally with the toe force compatible with the toe penetration (UFC 6-5.8.4.3, Fig 6-19). 'force_equilibrium' (the curves' intersection only; error if they do not intersect); 'settlement_compatibility' (pile and soil settle equally, toe force compatible with the toe penetration); 'bearing_layer_top' (top of the bearing layer, end-bearing pile, UFC 6-7.4 step 5); 'pile_toe' (whole shaft in negative skin friction, upper bound); 'endo' (Endo et al. 1969, CGPR #56 Table 3.1 fraction of the embedment; needs endo_bearing_condition). allowed: auto, force_equilibrium, settlement_compatibility, bearing_layer_top, pile_toe, endo default: "auto"
toe_mobilizationfloatoptionalFraction (0-1) of the nominal toe resistance mobilized where the load and resistance curves intersect. 1.0 = UFC 6-7.4 step 3 full mobilization ('a conservative approach for evaluating the drag force'); 0.5 and 0 = the other UFC 6-5.8.4.2 / GEC-12 7.3.6.1 cases for settlement (all three always reported in the comparison). default: 1.0
endo_bearing_conditionstringoptionalCGPR #56 Table 3.1 condition for Endo et al. (1969). allowed: floating, stiff_flexible, end_bearing
skin_friction_stressstringoptionalEffective stress for Beta-method skin friction (sand, and clay with skin_friction_method 'beta') and the sand toe: 'final' (default; sigma'v0 + fill/drawdown change, as UFC 3-220-20 6-7.4 step 2 requires) or 'initial' (sigma'v0). allowed: final, initial default: "final"
influence_depth_criterionstringoptionalHow deep below the toe the toe load is counted in the settlement (toe force spread 2V:1H from an equivalent footing as wide as the pile): to where its stress increase falls below 'bearing_stress' (default) = 10% of the bearing stress of the equivalent footing (UFC 3-220-20 6-5.8.4.3; 2.16 pile widths for a single pile) or 'effective_stress' = 10% of the existing vertical effective stress (FHWA GEC-12 Vol I step 1c: 7.3.5.3 for clay below the toe, 7.3.5.6 for sand, 7.3.5.5 for both; deeper for a loaded toe in soft soil). Either way the fill / drawdown, which does not decay with depth, compresses the settling layers below the toe down to the bottom of the soil profile; give the profile down to the base of the compressible soil. allowed: bearing_stress, effective_stress default: "bearing_stress"
influence_depth_warning_percentfloatoptionalThe result warns when the two influence_depth_criterion rules (UFC 3-220-20 6-5.8.4.3 and FHWA GEC-12 step 1c) give pile head settlements or drag forces that differ by more than this percentage of the larger of the two (of allowable_settlement / structural_capacity where given), and whenever a settlement or structural check passes with one rule and fails with the other. The rule used is not changed. Default 25 %: the engineer's call, not a reference's figure; neither reference says how far two settlement estimates may differ before it matters. default: 25.0
alpha_chartstringoptionalWhere a cohesive layer's alpha comes from when the layer leaves it out (a given alpha is kept). 'ufc_fig_6_14' (default; UFC 3-220-20 6-5.4.2, pp. 415-417, as its drag example App. B-5.4 reads it): soft clay (su below 800 psf) alpha 1 by Table 6-16; firm to very stiff clay off Fig 6-14 by su/Pa, curve A at Z of 40b or more, curve B at Z = 10b, linear between, Z from the ground surface to the clay's base or the pile toe and b = pile_diameter. 'gec12_fig_7_17': FHWA GEC-12 7.2.1.3.2 Step 1, Ca off Fig. 7-17 by su, D/b and fig_7_17_curve, as drawn (Ca may exceed su). choices states each clay's alpha and where it came from. Refused (with fig_7_17_curve and alpha_transition_zone) where no cohesive layer along the pile leaves alpha out. allowed: ufc_fig_6_14, gec12_fig_7_17 default: "ufc_fig_6_14"
fig_7_17_curvestringoptionalWith alpha_chart 'gec12_fig_7_17' only, and then required where a clay leaves alpha out: the Fig. 7-17 curves for the pile, 'concrete_timber_corrugated' (concrete, timber or corrugated steel; an H-pile takes the corrugated curve, GEC-12 Vol I p. 247) or 'smooth_steel'. allowed: concrete_timber_corrugated, smooth_steel
alpha_transition_zonebooloptionalWhether the top 10 pile widths of a stiff or very stiff clay (su 1500 psf or more) directly under soft clay take UFC 3-220-20 Eq 6-9, alpha = 0.28 (su/Pa)^-0.44 with the unit side resistance at least the soft clay's, and under sand alpha 1.0 (pp. 416-417, as App. B-5.4 does). Left out: true with alpha_chart 'ufc_fig_6_14', false with 'gec12_fig_7_17'. Applies only where the stiff clay's alpha is left out; refused where no such clay lies under soft clay or sand. The zone runs 10 pile widths from the top of the stiff clay however it is split into layers.
ground_elevationfloatoptionalElevation of the ground surface the depths are measured from (m): the top of the layers, where the pile head is taken (the original ground under a fill). Figures only: the calc package's profiles are drawn against elevation; every result stays in depth and no number changes.

                },
                {

                        "unit_weight": 19.0,
                        "phi": 34.0,

                }
        ],
        "Q_dead": 400.0,
        "fill_thickness": 2.0,
        "fill_unit_weight": 19.0,

    },
)

Applicability limits & conventions
  • For an H-pile pass the box toe area as pile_area; it is also the area used for AE and the pile weight. The module’s own shaft is the α-method in clay (UFC 3-220-20 Table 6-16, Fig. 6-14) and β from GEC-12 Table 7-9 in sand; it can differ from a Nordlund shaft, so give each layer’s β or α to reproduce a design shaft (as V-004 does).

4.3 Earth retention & excavation support

Walls that hold back soil and the systems that keep an excavation open and stable.

4.3.1 sheet_pile — Sheet-pile walls

Problems it solves

Cantilever and single-anchor flexible retaining walls: the embedment for stability, the maximum bending moment, and the anchor force, from a layered earth-pressure diagram with groundwater.

Methods & theories implemented
  • Rankine / Coulomb active and passive coefficients (with wall friction), and a log-spiral passive option (Coulomb active with it), which avoids Coulomb’s over-prediction of Kp at high δ: UFC 3-220-20 Eq. 4-12 by default, or Figs. 4-12/4-13 or the Caquot–Kerisel (1948) chart (Caltrans T&S Fig. 4-20); wall friction from UFC Table 4-1 by the soil against the wall.
  • The cantilever by the Caltrans T&S Simplified Method (Sec. 7-5.02): moments about the pivot O give D0, with the passive pressure divided by FOS_passive (UFC 3-220-20 Fig. 4-41 step 2), then D = 1.2 D0 (Caltrans 7-5.02 step 3; UFC Fig. 4-41 step 6); the maximum moment at zero shear on that factored diagram, to O. The anchored wall by free earth support about the anchor (UFC Fig. 4-37). Layered pressures with water on each side: water standing in the excavation above the dredge line counts, and the net water pressure is the retained side’s less the excavated side’s (UFC Sec. 4-4.1, Figs. 4-5/4-6).
  • References: Caltrans T&S Manual; UFC 3-220-20 (DM 7.2); USS Steel Sheet Piling Design Manual; validated against Caltrans T&S Ex 7-2’s layered pressures (V-025), Ex 8-1’s Ka and log-spiral Kp (V-013; that example’s embedment uses the FHWA apparent diagram, which soe reproduces), UFC Fig. 4-43 with water on both sides and, for the anchored wall’s maximum moment, the USS Steel Sheet Piling Design Manual’s Design Example No. 2 (within 1 %).

Sheet Pile
MethodWhat it doesParams
cantilever_wallCantilever sheet pile wall: embedment depth and maximum moment.9
anchored_wallAnchored sheet pile wall: embedment, anchor force, and moment.9
Parameters of cantilever_wall
ParameterTypeDescription
excavation_depthfloatrequiredExcavation depth (m).
layersarrayrequiredArray of soil-layer dicts, top down: {thickness (m, required), unit_weight (kN/m3, required; alias gamma), friction_angle (deg, default 30; alias phi), cohesion (kPa, default 0), wall_friction_deg (deg, 0 to friction_angle; alias delta), interface_soil (the soil against the steel, a row of the steel sheet pile wall friction table printed in UFC 3-220-20 Table 4-1, p. 184, EM 1110-2-2504 Table 3-3, p. 3-4, and the USS Steel Sheet Piling Design Manual Table 4, p. 13: 'clean_gravel' 22 deg (clean gravel, gravel-sand mixtures, well-graded rock fill with spalls), 'clean_sand' 17 (clean sand, silty sand-gravel mixture, single size hard rock fill), 'silty_sand' 14 (silty sand, gravel or sand mixed with silt or clay), 'fine_sandy_silt' 11 (fine sandy silt, nonplastic silt); at most friction_angle; not with wall_friction_deg)}. wall_friction_deg or interface_soil is used on both sides by pressure_method 'coulomb' and 'log_spiral'. A layer giving neither takes, with 'log_spiral', the clean_sand row (17 deg, at most its phi') on the passive side when it has no cohesion and no wall friction on the active side or in a layer with cohesion (UFC 3-220-20 Fig. 4-37 step 1, p. 237: 'Passive pressures for clean coarse grained soils include wall friction (see Table 4-1)'; it ignores wall friction in other soils, so give wall_friction_deg 0 in a silty sand or silt); with 'coulomb' none (UFC 3-220-20 p. 190: passive pressure 'should be calculated using the log spiral method and not the Coulomb method'). The result's choices give each layer's wall friction and its Kp at the other rows and at delta = 0, and where a layer took the clean sand row by default the embedment with none.
surchargefloatoptionalSurface surcharge (kPa). default: 0.0
FOS_passivefloatoptionalFOS applied to passive resistance. default: 1.5
gwt_depth_activefloatoptionalGroundwater depth on the active (retained) side, m below the top of the wall.
gwt_depth_passivefloatoptionalGroundwater depth on the passive (excavated) side, m below the top of the wall, the same datum as gwt_depth_active. A depth less than excavation_depth is water standing in front of the wall above the dredge line: its pressure, gamma_w times the depth below that level, acts on the wall from there down (UFC 3-220-20 Sec. 4-4.1, p. 199: 'Water applies a triangular pressure distribution equivalent to a soil with a unit weight of 62.4 pcf and an earth pressure coefficient of unity') and the soil below the dredge line is submerged (Fig. 4-41, p. 242: water levels can differ on the two sides; its example Fig. 4-43, p. 245, has water 5 ft below the top on both sides). The net water pressure is the retained side's less this side's (Figs. 4-5 and 4-6, p. 183: 'Net water pressure = u = gamma_w z2'), so the same depth on both sides (balanced water) gives none. Left out: the excavation level, or gwt_depth_active where that is deeper (no water on either side when gwt_depth_active is left out too), so no water stands in front of the wall.
pressure_methodstroptionalEarth pressure theory. 'log_spiral' uses Coulomb active + the log-spiral PASSIVE coefficient from log_spiral_source (avoids Coulomb's over-prediction of Kp at high delta/phi). 'coulomb' and 'log_spiral' take each layer's wall friction (layers: wall_friction_deg or interface_soil; what a layer giving neither takes is in the layers description). allowed: rankine, coulomb, log_spiral also read as: caquot_kerisel = log_spiral, logspiral = log_spiral default: "rankine"
log_spiral_sourcestroptionalWith pressure_method 'log_spiral', the printed source of the passive Kp. 'ufc_3_220_20' (default): UFC 3-220-20 (DM 7.2), the source the wall's geometry calls for (pp. 191-193); a sheet pile has a vertical face and the tool takes level ground in front of it, so that is Eq. 4-12 (p. 191), at each layer's wall_friction_deg. 'caquot_kerisel_1948': the Caquot and Kerisel (1948) chart, Kp at delta = phi times the printed reduction factor R(delta/phi), Caltrans Trenching and Shoring Manual Fig. 4-20 (p. 4-30), the method its Sec. 4-6 uses for passive pressure. 'dm7_2_fig_4_12', 'dm7_2_fig_4_13': UFC 3-220-20 Figs. 4-12 (p. 192, theta = 0 curve) and 4-13 (p. 193, beta = 0 row), Kerisel and Absi (1990), drawn for delta/phi' = 0.66 only, so every layer's wall_friction_deg must be 0.66 x its friction_angle; UFC 3-220-20 p. 260 says Kp for a tied-back wall 'should be obtained from Figure 4-12'. 'dm7_2_eq_4_12': Eq. 4-12 by name. They differ: at phi 30, delta/phi 0.66 the 1948 chart gives 5.4, the UFC charts 5.3 and Eq. 4-12 5.1. UFC 3-220-20 footnote 21 (p. 191): the 1982 DM 7.2 charts 'used delta/phi' = 1 along with reduction ratios', which 'were averages that introduced substantial inaccuracy for some cases'; the 1948 chart takes that form (Kp at delta = phi times R). UFC 3-220-20 Table 4-2 (p. 194) is not used: the log-spiral Kp in its row headed delta/phi' = 0.5, 5.3, 8.0, 12 and 20 at phi' = 30, 35, 40 and 45, are Fig. 4-13's values, drawn for delta/phi' = 0.66 (5.30, 8.00, 12.0, 20), and the Coulomb Kp printed beside them, 6.1, 9.8, 18 and 44, are Coulomb's at delta = 0.66 phi' (at 0.5 it gives 5.0, 7.4, 11.8 and 21.4). Eq. 4-12 at delta/phi' = 0.5 gives 4.46, 6.33, 9.33 and 14.3. The tool reads Fig. 4-13 at the 0.66 it is drawn for and Eq. 4-12 at the wall friction given. The result's choices give each layer's Kp from the source used and from the others. allowed: ufc_3_220_20, caquot_kerisel_1948, dm7_2_eq_4_12, dm7_2_fig_4_12, dm7_2_fig_4_13 default: "ufc_3_220_20"
embedment_increasefloatoptionalD / D0, the multiplier on the embedment from moment equilibrium: 1.2 (default), as the Caltrans Trenching and Shoring Manual (7-5.02 step 3, p. 7-11: 'The 20 percent increase is not a factor of safety'; its Example 7-3 takes it after FS 1.3 on the moments) and UFC 3-220-20 (Fig. 4-41 step 6, p. 242: 'Increase D by 20% to allow for dredging, scour, etc.'; its example Fig. 4-43 takes it after phi'allow = atan(tan 35 deg / 1.5) = 25 deg, Kp 3.6) both print it beside a factor of safety on the passive side. FOS_passive divides the passive pressure, UFC Fig. 4-41 step 2's alternative to phi'allow. Must be >= 1.0. default: 1.2
Worked example

Ask → A cantilever sheet pile retains a 4 m excavation in sand (φ=32°) with a 10 kPa surcharge. What embedment is needed and what is the maximum moment?

call_agent(
    agent_name='sheet_pile',
    method='cantilever_wall',
    parameters={
        "excavation_depth": 4.0,
        "layers": [
                {
                        "thickness": 15.0,
                        "unit_weight": 18.0,
                        "friction_angle": 32.0,
                        "cohesion": 0.0
                }
        ],
        "surcharge": 10.0,
        "FOS_passive": 1.5,
        "embedment_increase": 1.2
    },
)

Applicability limits & conventions
  • analyze_cantilever is the Caltrans Simplified Method for a continuous wall, per metre run: soldier-pile effective widths and arching (Caltrans T&S Ch. 7) are not modelled (V-012). It is not UFC 3-220-20 Fig. 4-41’s full method, which gives a longer D: on UFC Fig. 4-43, 15.6 ft against the chart’s 17 ft. The maximum moment is on the factored diagram (UFC Fig. 4-41 step 5); soe’s cantilever takes it at FS 1.0 (Caltrans Ex 7-3), so the two tools differ.

4.3.2 soe — Support of excavation

Problems it solves

Support of an open excavation: braced and cantilever walls, apparent-pressure diagrams, strut/anchor loads, wall-section selection, and the bottom-stability checks (basal heave, blowout, piping).

Methods & theories implemented
  • FHWA apparent-pressure envelopes (Terzaghi–Peck / Peck) for braced cuts and anchored walls; braced-wall support loads by the Caltrans hinge method (or GEC-4's, or UFC 3-220-20's simple spans) and the GEC-4 tributary area method for anchored walls.
  • The cantilever by the Caltrans T&S Simplified Method (Sec. 7-5.02; D = 1.2 D0; moment and shear at FS 1.0, Ex 7-3); the embedment below the lowest support of a braced or anchored wall, one support or several, by free earth support about it (Sec. 8-4.02); ground-anchor design by GEC-4 Sec. 5.3; wall-section sizing at 0.60 Fy by default (the Caltrans examples).
  • Basal heave — Terzaghi (the default; GEC-4 Eq. 35 with side shear, Eq. 37 for a wide cut, Nc off GEC-4 Fig. 51(c); UFC 3-220-20 Fig. 2-7(b) given beside it), Bjerrum–Eide (Nc off Caltrans Fig. 10-15 with Eq. 10-3-4) and the Caltrans force balance with sidewall shear (Sec. 10-3.01); bottom blowout (soil-plug weight against the excess head) and piping (critical gradient against the average exit gradient), in the module’s own forms, since none of these references prints one.
  • References: FHWA GEC-4 (FHWA-IF-99-015); Terzaghi & Peck; Bjerrum & Eide; Caltrans T&S; validated V-014/V-016.
